title: Massive Disruption Now: What AI Means for Students, Educators, Administrators and Accreditation Boards
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard argues that educators have been slow to grasp where generative AI is heading and that K-16 institutions must plan now for AI tutors that hallucinate less, write in student voices, do math and adapt to each learner at a fraction of a teacher's cost. He walks through the consequences for students, teachers, administrators and accreditation bodies: uncontrolled AI-assisted writing, cyborg students and instructors, decentralised learning, changed assessment, and pressure on weaker universities. The bulk of the piece is a long list of recommendations, including AI literacy, professional development, a Head of AI, a short AI policy framework, de-emphasising plagiarism policing, and teaching soft skills. He balances this with reminders that students still need knowledge and that current systems provide some useful sorting. The tone is urgent and the timelines are speculative, and the author promotes his own consultancy, but it is a comprehensive 2023 artifact of the pro-adoption AI-in-education position.
points: The central claim is that institutions planning around 2022-era AI will be obsolete within a few years, so strategy must assume capable, personalised AI tutors.
AI detectors are a failing and discriminatory response; assessment must be redesigned and an anti-plagiarism stance cannot be an institution's whole AI policy.
Teachers are expected to move toward a coaching role in a student-teacher-AI conversation, so teacher preparation and professional development need to change.
Concrete moves for schools include AI literacy, requiring AI use in at least one assignment, hiring a Head of AI, and hosting open round tables.
Despite the urgency, the author concedes students still need content knowledge and that the existing system provides useful signals about diligence and ability.
quotes: The problem, however, is that they didn’t stay the same (they’ve already reduced these problems), and what AIs will be in two years or less, is nothing short of world-changing. While education may have been able to “push through” ChatGPT3.5, and even manage to avoid change in a world of ChatGPT4, both new tools and a recognition of their future means this is something education can longer ignore and many educators are coming around (if slowly).

Fall 2026 is three years away. Do you have a three year plan? Perhaps you should scrap it and write a new one (or at least realize that your current one cannot survive). If you run an academic institution in 2026 the same way you ran it in 2022, you might as well run it like you would have in 1920.

Educators who understand AI, including how to use it and teach with it in their field, will be the ones who are the best teachers. They will be providing the most relevant instruction, they will attract students who are worried about their future and they will produce the most dynamic and engaging classroom environments and relevant assessments. Educator cyborgs who use AI properly will simply run circles around colleagues who try to teach with pre-AI world tools and with assessments designed for that era.

More and more people say this will shift to a “coaching” model (Fitzpatrick; me in January 2023: “Educators as Coaches”), where the teacher facilitates learning in a three way conversation between student, teacher, and AI. Teachers may not lose their jobs, but the nature of what we need K-12 teachers to do will change and individuals who can adapt to this environment will be the best (and perhaps the only) teachers.

It means assessments have to change. Single-artifact assignments can be done better by AIs than by students (or at least soon they will be able to). Trying to use AI detectors to stop student use is not only a recipe for failure but deprives students of real-world skills.

Stopping student plagiarism in these instances is important, but an anti-AI plagiarism policy cannot be your AI policy. Do you want to be the school that hires a Head of AI or do you want to be the school that spends all day fighting student plagiarism? When you work on your institution’s AI policy/guidelines, you should spend (at most) 5% of your time on how you will manage plagiarism.

I don’t know anyone who doesn’t think students need basic math and science skills and subjects such as history are important to bind students to country and culture. English and humanities courses are needed to help students think through the essential elements of what it means to be human.
